# Incident Report: PCAP Traffic Analysis — 2022-01-07

## Victim Host
| Field | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | **192.168.1.216** | Top talker in `ip conv`; source of all suspicious traffic |
| MAC | **9c:5c:8e:32:58:f9** (ASUSTek NIC) | ARP replies for 192.168.1.216; bound in DHCP request (frame 1) |
| Hostname | **DESKTOP-GXMYNO2** | DHCP option 12 (frame 1), Kerberos `CNameString` (`desktop-gxmyno2$`), NTLMSSP hostname field, mDNS/LLMNR queries — 71 occurrences of this exact string across the capture |
| Logged-in user | **steve.smith** (domain `SPOONWATCH`, realm `SPOONWATCH.NET`) | Kerberos `CNameString` and NTLMSSP `ntlmssp.auth.username`/`ntlmssp.auth.domain` in SMB2 session setup to the DC |

Domain controller for context: `SPOONWATCH-DC` at 192.168.1.2 (MAC `20:47:47:62:ae:26`), confirmed via NBNS, LDAP/CLDAP, Kerberos, and DNS SRV records. This traffic is benign AD authentication activity, not part of the compromise.

## Malware Family
**Vidar Stealer** — attribution is **behavioral**, not signature-confirmed (no IDS/Suricata alert file was present in the evidence directory; the pcap was the only artifact).

Behavioral basis:
- The victim beacons directly to a **bare IP address, 2.56.57.108, over port 80**, with **no preceding DNS query resolving to that IP anywhere in the capture** — a hardcoded C2 address.
- All requests carry a static, non-browser-realistic header set: `Accept-Language: ru-RU,ru;q=0.9,en;q=0.8`, `Accept-Charset: iso-8859-1, utf-8, utf-16, *;q=0.1`, `Accept: ... image/x-xbitmap, */*;q=0.1` — a known hardcoded Vidar HTTP fingerprint.
- The host sends 7 empty (25-byte) `multipart/form-data` POST check-ins to `/osk//1.jpg` through `/osk//7.jpg`, `/osk//main.php`, and finally `/osk/`, all to the same IP/port.
- The server responds to each `N.jpg` request with `Content-Type: image/jpeg`, but the actual bytes are **Win32 PE DLLs**, not images. Export and identification of these 7 files shows they are exactly the canonical Vidar support-DLL bundle used to read browser credential stores: `sqlite3.dll`, `freebl3.dll`, `nss3.dll`, `softokn3.dll`, `nssdbm3.dll`, `mozglue.dll`, `msvcp140.dll`, `vcruntime140.dll`.
- The final POST to `/osk/` (379,629 bytes, `Content-Length` matches) uploads a `multipart/form-data` file named **`_5861695120.zip`**. Extracting it shows the classic Vidar exfiltration archive layout: `autofill/`, `cc/`, `cookies/` (Chrome + Edge), `outlook.txt`, `passwords.txt`, `screenshot.jpg`, `system.txt`.
- Server banner on all responses: `Apache/2.4.12 (Win32) OpenSSL/1.0.1m PHP/5.3.29 mod_wsgi/4.4.11 Python/2.7.10`.

The combination of a hardcoded-IP C2, disguised DLL downloads matching Vidar's specific 7-file NSS/SQLite bundle, and an exfil zip with Vidar's characteristic folder structure is strong, consistent behavioral evidence for Vidar Stealer. The capture begins at system boot (DHCP request) and the first C2 beacon fires only ~203 seconds later, so no delivery/dropper chain (phishing, initial download) is visible in this pcap — Vidar was already resident and triggered on startup or logon.

## Indicators of Compromise

**C2 endpoint**
- `2.56.57.108:80` — evidence: TCP conversation `192.168.1.216:49738 <-> 2.56.57.108:80`, 3335 frames / 3598 kB, all HTTP request/response traffic described above.

**Domains**
- None grounded. No DNS query in the capture resolves to 2.56.57.108; the malware uses a hardcoded IP.

**URLs**
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//1.jpg` through `/osk//7.jpg` — GET-equivalent (via POST check-in) payload delivery for the 7 disguised DLLs (frames 1501, 1641, 2225, 2541, 2691, 3054, 4194).
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//main.php` — POST check-in, empty 25-byte multipart body, `text/html` 0-byte response (frame 4275).
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk/` — final POST exfiltrating the stolen-data archive (frame 4816).

**Transferred files / hashes** (all served with a spoofed `image/jpeg` Content-Type, all confirmed PE32 DLLs by file magic):

| URI | Delivered as | SHA256 |
|---|---|---|
| /osk//1.jpg | sqlite3.dll | `16574f51785b0e2fc29c2c61477eb47bb39f714829999511dc8952b43ab17660` |
| /osk//2.jpg | freebl3.dll / nss3.dll | `a770ecba3b08bbabd0a567fc978e50615f8b346709f8eb3cfacf3faab24090ba` |
| /osk//3.jpg | mozglue.dll | `3fe6b1c54b8cf28f571e0c5d6636b4069a8ab00b4f11dd842cfec00691d0c9cd` |
| /osk//4.jpg | msvcp140.dll / vcruntime140.dll | `334e69ac9367f708ce601a6f490ff227d6c20636da5222f148b25831d22e13d4` |
| /osk//5.jpg | mozglue.dll / nss3.dll / softokn3.dll | `e2935b5b28550d47dc971f456d6961f20d1633b4892998750140e0eaa9ae9d78` |
| /osk//6.jpg | freebl3.dll / nss3.dll / nssdbm3.dll / softokn3.dll | `43536adef2ddcc811c28d35fa6ce3031029a2424ad393989db36169ff2995083` |
| /osk//7.jpg | vcruntime140.dll | `c40bb03199a2054dabfc7a8e01d6098e91de7193619effbd0f142a7bf031c14d` |
| /osk/ (exfil upload) | `_5861695120.zip` (stolen-data archive: autofill, cookies, passwords.txt, outlook.txt, screenshot.jpg, system.txt) | `5d4be98187cae207e49d4c326d00510e461f054d0f7c28066468100534483851` |

## Benign Context (not indicators)
- `192.168.1.2` / `spoonwatch-dc.spoonwatch.net` — internal AD domain controller (LDAP, CLDAP, Kerberos, SMB2, DRSUAPI traffic).
- `192.168.1.1` — LAN gateway/DHCP server.
- `23.38.189.225`, `23.38.189.201`, `8.253.189.126` — Akamai-hosted `download.windowsupdate.com` / `ctldl.windowsupdate.com`, legitimate Windows Update .cab and definition-update traffic.
- `52.249.36.204`, `52.178.17.2`, `52.183.220.149`, `52.168.112.67`, `20.189.173.1`, `20.54.89.15`, `20.50.80.210`, `52.179.216.235`, `104.212.67.47`, `40.83.240.146` — Microsoft telemetry/services endpoints (`*.events.data.microsoft.com`, `client.wns.windows.com`, `pti.store.microsoft.com`, `cp801/kv801.prod.do.dsp.mp.microsoft.com`, etc.), all TLS SNI-confirmed.
- `204.79.197.200`, `204.79.197.203` — `www.bing.com`, `api.msn.com` (Windows default widgets/search telemetry).
- `224.0.0.22`, `224.0.0.251`, `224.0.0.252`, `239.255.255.250` — IGMP/mDNS/LLMNR/SSDP local multicast noise.

## Incident Summary
The Windows workstation DESKTOP-GXMYNO2 (192.168.1.216, MAC 9c:5c:8e:32:58:f9), logged in as domain user SPOONWATCH\steve.smith, was infected with Vidar Stealer. Roughly 3.5 minutes after boot, the malware began beaconing to a hardcoded C2 at 2.56.57.108:80, downloaded 7 support DLLs disguised as JPEG files under `/osk/` to read Chrome/Edge/NSS credential stores, and exfiltrated a ZIP archive (`_5861695120.zip`) of stolen autofill data, cookies, saved passwords, Outlook data, a screenshot, and system information back to the same C2. No initial-infection artifact (dropper, phishing document, or delivery download) appears in this capture, so the delivery vector could not be determined from this evidence alone.
